newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb army says dispute not resolved.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb army says dispute not resolved.

text.p: Bosnian Serb army officers denied early on Tuesday that they had reached any agreement with their political leaders who have tried to purge the general staff.

The army headquarters under commander General Ratko Mladic issued a stern statement saying civilian-controlled media had distorted the results of a meeting on Monday with Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic.
Serb media reported late on Monday that Plavsic had reached an agreement with ousted generals on transferring authority to new commanders.
But the army's account indicated that more than seven hours of talks in the northwest city of Banja Luka had failed to produce a deal between Plavsic and six top generals.
Mladic's headquarters said only the commander himself should decide on changes to the military leadership.
The statement proposed that Plavsic meet Mladic on Wednesday to discuss the dispute.
Until Tuesday, the army has tended to avoid using Mladic's name since the Bosnian war ended last year.

Mladic, who has kept a low profile over the past year, has been charged with genocide by a U.N. war crimes tribunal and must step down from any public post under terms of the U.S.-brokered peace treaty.
A power struggle has erupted since Plavsic's decision last week to dismiss General Mladic and the rest of his general staff -- a move the army has so far refused to recognise.
Until the dispute was settled, the army said new commanders recently appointed by civilian authorities would not be allowed to visit any army base without "permission and knowledge" of Mladic.
In the meantime, the army vowed to fight against any bid to enforce the dismissals.
"Any attempt at a forced replacement of officers and troops should be vigorously resisted," it said.
Political analysts say wartime leader Radovan Karadzic is almost certainly behind the move to dismiss the general staff.
Karadzic, who resigned as president under international pressure in July, tried and failed to sack Mladic and other top generals last year.
The order to sack Mladic appeared to be an attempt by civilian authorities to settle the long-running rift between politicians and the army once and for all.
The army has accused civilian leaders of corruption and war profiteering and the politicians have accused the army of kowtowing to the Bosnian Serbs' patrons in neighbouring Serbia.
The two sides traded insults through the media over the weekend, with Mladic's officers dismissing the newly appointed commanders as lightweight party hacks.
